claims.text: Conventional high-temperature synthesis produces NM-HEAs with ambiguous atomic arrangements.
Conventional rapid-mixing synthesis produces nonuniform NM-HEA nanostructures.
A machine-learning model trained on experimental and atomistic-simulation data can predict and tune NM-HEA synthesis parameters in real time.
Temperature influences atomic diffusion and phase evolution in noble-metal-containing high-entropy nanoalloys.
In situ aberration-corrected STEM can monitor atomic-scale structural and chemical changes during heating of high-entropy nanoalloys.
In situ STEM can monitor the proposed nanoframework synthesis under catalytic operating conditions.
ML-guided synthesis will produce an interconnected three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework will exhibit a uniform atomic distribution.
The resulting nanoframework will have a high density of well-defined active sites.
Statistical correlations learned by the ML model can precisely control atomic diffusion in NM-HEAs.
Statistical correlations learned by the ML model can precisely control phase evolution in NM-HEAs.
ML-guided control of diffusion and phase evolution will prevent elemental segregation and undesired mixed phases.
Preventing segregation and undesired mixed phases will promote the desired three-dimensional nanoframework architecture.
ML-optimized protocols will improve the atomic precision of NM-HEA nanoframeworks relative to conventional synthesis.
ML-optimized protocols will increase active-site density relative to conventional synthesis.
Improved atomic precision and active-site density will produce superior catalytic performance.
The effectiveness of the ML-guided approach depends on the accuracy and coverage of available experimental and simulation data.
The proposed approach may face scalability and processing-environment variability limitations.
